{"id": "20:44/q11", "question": "What does the hope clause attach to grammatically?", "turns_on": "The question is whether the clause modifies the command to speak or the earlier command to go.", "positions": [{"id": "20:44/q11/p1", "position": "It is circumstantial to the implied dual subject of 'speak.'", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī prefers attachment to قولا and says أو keeps both outcomes possible."}, {"id": "20:44/q11/p2", "position": "It is circumstantial to the dual subject of the earlier 'go.'", "reasons": "Al-Bayḍāwī allows attachment to ذهبا or قولا; al-Ālūsī reports the former but prefers the latter."}]}
{"id": "20:44/q12", "question": "What does يَتَذَكَّرُ mean?", "turns_on": "The glosses vary between intellectual recognition, recollection of lordship, and practical repentance.", "positions": [{"id": "20:44/q12/p1", "position": "Reflect on the reminder and acknowledge the truth, yielding to it.", "reasons": "Al-Zamakhsharī, Abū Ḥayyān, and al-Ālūsī describe reflection leading to fairness. Al-Biqāʿī specifies God's care through Pharaoh's changing life stages. Ibn ʿĀshūr says recognition corrects his false confidence. Ṭabāṭabāʾī makes it acceptance of the reminder, proof, and faith."}, {"id": "20:44/q12/p2", "position": "Recall God's lordship and his own servitude.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabrisī defines the mission's desired recollection this way."}, {"id": "20:44/q12/p3", "position": "Turn back from forbidden conduct or misguidance.", "reasons": "Ibn Kathīr contrasts this with fear as attaining obedience and cites 87:10; the Study Quran reports heeding the warning or turning from misguidance."}]}
{"id": "20:44/q13", "question": "What does يَخْشَىٰ mean?", "turns_on": "The notes differ over fear from a possibly true warning, fear of God leading to obedience, and fear of divine power.", "positions": [{"id": "20:44/q13/p1", "position": "Fear that the warning is true and denial may bring punishment or ruin.", "reasons": "Al-Zamakhsharī, al-Nasafī, Abū Ḥayyān, al-Biqāʿī, and al-Ālūsī stress fear despite incomplete certainty. Al-Biqāʿī says it might lead Pharaoh to release Israel. Ibn ʿĀshūr calls this cautious compliance. Al-Ālūsī prefers it to a generic account of divine punishment."}, {"id": "20:44/q13/p2", "position": "Fear God, submit, and become obedient to Him.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabrisī connects fear with the threatened punishment; al-Baghawī says fear and submission to Islam. Ibn Kathīr defines fear as attaining obedience, citing 87:10. The Study Quran says fear may return Pharaoh to God. Al-Burṣawī links reverent fear especially with the learned, citing 35:28."}, {"id": "20:44/q13/p3", "position": "Become wary of God's power and punishment.", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī reports this explanation but favors fear that the messengers' warning may be true."}]}
{"id": "20:44/q14", "question": "Why is remembering mentioned before fearing?", "turns_on": "The disagreement concerns whether fear is the lesser response after recognition is offered, or a stage leading toward it.", "positions": [{"id": "20:44/q14/p1", "position": "Recognition and wholehearted acceptance come first; fear of a possibly true warning is a lesser fallback.", "reasons": "Al-Bayḍāwī says remembrance follows recognized truth, fear suspected truth. Rāzī ranks persistent truth, suspension, and persistent falsehood and says either improvement beats Pharaoh's fixed rejection. Al-Ālūsī calls remembrance the response of the grounded."}, {"id": "20:44/q14/p2", "position": "Fear can precede full acceptance, so either may bring Pharaoh toward faith.", "reasons": "Ṭabāṭabāʾī says fear comes before acceptance of the reminder, making the pair 'believe or approach belief and answer them.'"}]}
{"id": "20:44/q15", "question": "What does أَوْ do between the two outcomes?", "turns_on": "Some read the conjunction as additive; others retain two possible outcomes, while the lexical notes also discuss ordinary uncertainty.", "positions": [{"id": "20:44/q15/p1", "position": "It is additive, equivalent to 'and.'", "reasons": "Al-Suddī, exegetes cited by Ibn Qutayba and Ibn al-Jawzī, al-Dāmghānī, al-Burhān, and al-Itqān take it this way. Examples include 77:6, 80:3, 20:113, a Jarīr verse and a Tawba verse. Ibn al-Jawzī also reports al-Farrāʾ's poetic 'rather' and ordinary choice, but those are general functions of أو, not asserted for this clause."}, {"id": "20:44/q15/p2", "position": "It permits either remembrance or fear as a sought outcome, without excluding both.", "reasons": "Al-Burhān says either outcome may be sought. Al-Irshād, quoted by al-Burṣawī, says أو excludes neither. Al-Ālūsī likewise says the particle prevents excluding either."}, {"id": "20:44/q15/p3", "position": "It can express uncertainty between alternatives.", "reasons": "Ibn Qutayba illustrates with seeing ʿAbd Allāh or Muḥammad; Ibn al-Jawzī gives Zayd or ʿAmr and also an ordinary choice between a coin and silver value. Al-Dāmghānī's excerpt begins a separate awwal entry on first unbelief and belief but gives no local application."}]}
{"id": "20:44/q16", "question": "Who might remember or fear?", "turns_on": "The pronoun's immediate target is Pharaoh, while reported readings transfer the hoped for response to witnesses.", "positions": [{"id": "20:44/q16/p1", "position": "Pharaoh himself.", "reasons": "This is the surface referent throughout the address; Muqātil and others explain the hope as his chance to heed."}, {"id": "20:44/q16/p2", "position": "A witness or others who hear and see God's gentleness.", "reasons": "Al-Ḥusayn ibn al-Faḍl says a witness might learn from kindness to the claimant of divinity; al-Nasafī reports 'a reminder may remember or a fearful person may fear,' adding that many did. Al-Tustarī names magicians and others whom God knows He will guide."}]}
{"id": "20:44/q17", "question": "Did Pharaoh remember or fear, and when?", "turns_on": "Reports place a response at drowning, before Hāmān's counsel, or in the Nile episode; another report emphasizes nonbelief.", "positions": [{"id": "20:44/q17/p1", "position": "He remembered, feared, and professed faith only while drowning, too late to benefit him.", "reasons": "Al-Warrāq, Muʿādh, Qurṭubī, al-Nasafī, and al-Burṣawī connect the response to 10:90. Al-Ālūsī rejects applying this late response to the clause, and rejects a salvation argument built from it."}, {"id": "20:44/q17/p2", "position": "He remembered and feared earlier, but Hāmān diverted him from following Moses.", "reasons": "Al-Nasafī says Pharaoh wanted to follow Moses but made no decision without Hāmān. Al-Baghawī and al-Ṭabrisī say he liked the offered youth, rule, pleasures, and Paradise until Hāmān shamed him as a deity becoming a subject. Qurṭubī adds that his believing wife urged faith, Hāmān offered to restore his youth and dyed his beard black, reportedly first to do so; Abū Ḥayyān names Āsiyah."}, {"id": "20:44/q17/p3", "position": "He prostrated when the Nile receded and might have recalled God's forbearance when it followed his horse.", "reasons": "Abū Ḥayyān and al-Ālūsī transmit this Nile episode; Abū Ḥayyān frames the hoped for remembrance and fear around divine generosity and punishment."}, {"id": "20:44/q17/p4", "position": "He was divinely fated not to believe.", "reasons": "Kaʿb's Torah report says God commanded gentle speech while announcing He would harden Pharaoh's heart. The theologians and commentators also discuss God's advance knowledge of nonbelief, without making it a narrative of prior remembrance."}]}
{"id": "20:44/q18", "question": "How many years were included in the reported promise to Pharaoh?", "turns_on": "The two reports give different numbers and differ over whether years are a matching lifespan or an addition.", "positions": [{"id": "20:44/q18/p1", "position": "A lifespan of 409 years, matching Pharaoh's reported age.", "reasons": "ʿAmr ibn Dīnār says Pharaoh lived 409 years and Moses promised him that lifespan and Paradise if he obeyed."}, {"id": "20:44/q18/p2", "position": "Four hundred extra years.", "reasons": "Qurṭubī reports this with youth, kingdom until death, and Paradise."}]}
{"id": "20:44/q19", "question": "Why send messengers when God knew Pharaoh would not believe?", "turns_on": "The accounts turn on proof, decree and command, divine knowledge, and whether people originate their acts.", "positions": [{"id": "20:44/q19/p1", "position": "Their mission establishes proof, removes excuse, and manifests the result before punishment.", "reasons": "Al-Zajjāj says divine knowledge alone cannot establish proof for humans. Al-Zamakhsharī cites 20:134; Abū Ḥayyān cites 17:15. Al-Burṣawī says message precedes punishment, while al-Taʾwīlāt al-Najmiyya says the mission establishes the messengers and makes Pharaoh's rejection manifest, citing 8:42."}, {"id": "20:44/q19/p2", "position": "The reason is a mystery before which reason should submit.", "reasons": "Rāzī asks why exhorting one known not to believe increases his liability, comparing it to handing a doomed person a knife. Al-Ālūsī endorses the Imam's submission."}, {"id": "20:44/q19/p3", "position": "A prescriptive command can differ from God's decree; fixed knowledge reveals capacities and outcomes.", "reasons": "Al-Burṣawī reports a distinction between command and decree, says a sinner can bear a duty without readiness to perform it, and treats the command as displaying felicity and misery. He quotes Ḥāfiẓ on surrender to a divinely directed course."}, {"id": "20:44/q19/p4", "position": "Divine foreknowledge of Pharaoh's freely chosen disbelief does not make belief impossible.", "reasons": "Al-Baḥr al-ʿUlūm says knowledge follows the known act as it is; al-Burṣawī argues the verse shows human capacity affects acts, against al-Ashʿarī's denial of such effect."}, {"id": "20:44/q19/p5", "position": "God intended Pharaoh and his people to remember, and human acts originate in the servant.", "reasons": "Jishumī uses لعل against determinists and argues that if God created each act, gentlen

{"id": "20:44/q20", "question": "What surrounding reports or scriptural links illuminate the mission?", "turns_on": "These are distinct reports about the mission rather than rival explanations of a single event.", "positions": [{"id": "20:44/q20/p1", "position": "Aaron met Moses on the way to Egypt after receiving inspiration.", "reasons": "Al-Baghawī says Aaron was in Egypt, God ordered Moses toward him, inspired Aaron to meet him, and they met after a day's journey."}, {"id": "20:44/q20/p2", "position": "The Torah reportedly commands gentle speech even though God will harden Pharaoh's heart.", "reasons": "Kaʿb swears to this Torah wording as cited by Ibn al-Jawzī and Rāzī."}, {"id": "20:44/q20/p3", "position": "Poetry depicts Moses and Aaron questioning Pharaoh about the Creator of heaven and earthly life.", "reasons": "Ibn Kathīr cites lines ascribed to Zayd ibn ʿAmr ibn Nufayl, alternatively to Umayya ibn Abī al-Ṣalt by Ibn Isḥāq."}, {"id": "20:44/q20/p4", "position": "Moses and Aaron should first give Pharaoh warning and a chance to respond.", "reasons": "Al-Ḥasan says they should not demand his destruction before giving him an excuse and warning."}]}
{"id": "20:45/q01", "question": "Who spoke the dual words قالا, and when?", "turns_on": "Whether Aaron had already joined Moses when the fear was expressed, and whether the dual reports a single shared utterance.", "positions": [{"id": "20:45/q01/p1", "position": "Moses and Aaron spoke together after they met and learned of the mission.", "reasons": "Ibn al-Jawzi reports Aaron was in Egypt, summoned to meet Moses; Qaffal says Moses may have paused until their meeting (20:36). Kashifi says Aaron heard Moses's story and warned of Pharaoh's power to kill or crucify. Islahi takes joint supplication as evidence that these directions followed their reunion in Egypt."}, {"id": "20:45/q01/p2", "position": "Moses spoke while Aaron was absent, and the dual includes Aaron as his partner.", "reasons": "Ibn al-Anbari notes Arabic dual address may include one person; Qaffal says Moses's leadership included Aaron and cites collective attribution in 2:72 and 63:8. Al-Irshad calls Moses primary and Aaron subordinate by grammatical predominance. Razi refers back to this explanation."}, {"id": "20:45/q01/p3", "position": "Both spoke together at Sinai.", "reasons": "Al-Alusi compares the collective attribution to the plural address to messengers in 23:51, which did not require each messenger to be addressed individually."}, {"id": "20:45/q01/p4", "position": "The verse combines Moses's earlier fear with Aaron's later fear, without requiring one occasion.", "reasons": "Tabatabai says Moses's fear could precede Aaron's receipt of the command."}]}
{"id": "20:45/q02", "question": "Is قالا transmitted in another number?", "turns_on": "The transmitted dual wording versus the singular codex reading.", "positions": [{"id": "20:45/q02/p1", "position": "The verse has dual 'they said'.", "reasons": "The ordinary dual wording underlies the explanations of both brothers speaking or of Aaron's inclusion in Moses's speech."}, {"id": "20:45/q02/p2", "position": "The codices of Ibn Masʿud and Hafsa have singular 'he said'.", "reasons": "Razi reports this reading and explains that Moses spoke for himself and his brother."}]}
{"id": "20:45/q03", "question": "Why does إننا emphatically state their fear?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "20:45/q03/p1", "position": "The added nūn intensifies the fear and complaint, preparing proportionate reassurance.", "reasons": "Al-Biqaʿi relates the intensified expression to the severity of their distress."}]}
{"id": "20:45/q04", "question": "What does نخاف denote in this setting?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "20:45/q04/p1", "position": "Fear is expectation of harm from signs that make it likely or known.", "reasons": "Bursevi contrasts fear with hope, expectation of a desired thing, and security; fear covers worldly and otherworldly matters (17:57). Fear of God means restraint from sin and obedience, rather than bodily terror."}]}
{"id": "20:45/q05", "question": "Why could Moses and Aaron fear Pharaoh despite their prophetic mission and assurances?", "turns_on": "Whether fear concerns their safety, completion of the message, or desire for reassurance, and how the timing and scope of the prior promise in 28:35 are understood.", "positions": [{"id": "20:45/q05/p1", "position": "They feared Pharaoh's physical harm or death as a real danger.", "reasons": "Jishumi says prophets fear enemies until reassured. Al-Biqaʿi stresses Pharaoh's great power and their need for divine protection. Asad says banishment or killing could cut off the message. Tabatabai says the earlier fear concerned Moses's life (26:14); al-Alusi notes early authorities support a physical-harm reading despite 28:35."}, {"id": "20:45/q05/p2", "position": "Their chief fear was interruption of the mission, rather than death for its own sake.", "reasons": "Razi says they trusted Pharaoh would not kill them but feared harm before or after delivery. Al-Taʾwilat al-Najmiyya says human fear persists in prophets but they feared failure in servitude. Al-Alusi reports that removal of this obstacle elaborates Moses's earlier request; Tabatabai distinguishes this verse from Moses's earlier personal fear. Asad names banishment or death before full delivery."}, {"id": "20:45/q05/p3", "position": "Fear can coexist with an expanded breast and patient resolve.", "reasons": "Razi explains expansion as capacity to preserve commands and laws without forgetfulness or distortion, not absence of fear. Al-Alusi reports that view but notes many take it as ease and patience in hardship; he says one may seek protection and still endure an affliction steadfastly. Kuranyolu favors responsibility's psychological burden over a physical speech defect and cites Moses's wish that his words be understood in 20:28."}, {"id": "20:45/q05/p4", "position": "They sought a further revealed assurance to reinforce their confidence.", "reasons": "Razi says rational grounds for confidence were strengthened by revelation, comparing Abraham's request in 2:260. Al-Alusi reports this explanation but rejects its claim that they already knew with certainty that nothing could interrupt delivery."}, {"id": "20:45/q05/p5", "position": "Their fear appears difficult to reconcile with a prior promise of protection.", "reasons": "The objectors cite the promise to strengthen Moses with Aaron and shield both (28:35). Al-Alusi says the promise may concern defeat in argument and that its timing is uncertain, while early authorities favor physical harm. Tabatabai treats their fear as unobjectionable."}, {"id": "20:45/q05/p6", "position": "The two fears may have arisen on separate occasions.", "reasons": "Tabatabai allows Moses's earlier private fear and Aaron's fear after receiving the command to be combined in one verse."}]}
{"id": "20:45/q06", "question": "What does their pause to express fear imply about a command's timing?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "20:45/q06/p1", "position": "An imperative alone does not require immediate performance.", "reasons": "Razi argues that, if immediacy were required, their delay after the command would strongly imply prophetic disobedience, which is excluded. Al-Alusi reports the Imam's same inference from the repeated commands."}]}
{"id": "20:45/q07", "question": "What action is feared in يَفْرُطَ عَلَيْنَا?", "turns_on": "Whether the verb denotes haste, excess, or induced haste, and whether Pharaoh or an elided act or statement is its subject.", "positions": [{"id": "20:45/q07/p1", "position": "Pharaoh may hasten to punish, attack, or kill them, especially before they finish presenting the message and signs.", "reasons": "Mujahid, Ibn Abbas, Ibn Zayd and others give punishment or killing; Ibn Zayd says it could follow immediately on conveying God's command (20:46). Tabari, Zajjaj, Ibn Qutayba, al-Asmaʿi, Ibn al-Aʿrabi, Zamakhshari, Abu Hayyan and others derive haste from farṭ, going ahead; fāriṭ precedes a party to water, a leading horse outruns others, rajaz and al-Qutami's verse illustrate it, and the Prophet says 'I precede you at the Pond.' Al-Kisaʾi lists verb forms; Kaʿb ibn Zuhayr uses afraṭa for arriving ahead of time. Islahi says ʿalaynā gives the force of sudden assault and notes Pharaoh's existing anger; Study Quran cites his swift execution of the sorcerers (20:70–73; 7:124). Wahidi refers to discussion at 16:62."}, {"id": "20:45/q07/p2", "position": "Pharaoh may exceed bounds in injuring or punishing them.", "reasons": "Tabari, al-Mubarrad, al-Farraʾ and Jishumi distinguish ifrāṭ as excess from tafrīṭ as shortcoming; Jishumi connects the root to advancing out of place or failing to advance. Al-Mubarrad compares punishment to one excessive in sin; Qurtubi also reports his view that Pharaoh punishes for supposed prior wrongdoing. The rajaz cited by Qurtubi uses afraṭa for overstepping and hurrying. This sense accompanies readings from ifrāṭ."}, {"id": "20:45/q07/p3", "position": "Something may impel Pharaoh to rush against them.", "reasons": "Zamakhshari and Razi list Satan, Pharaoh's divine claim and arrogance, love of rule, or rebellious Egyptian courtiers; Baydawi also mentions fear for rule and a human or jinn devil. Abu Hayyan cites 7:109 and 7:127. The passive or causative readings support the idea."}, {"id": "20:45/q07/p4", "position": "An act or statement from Pharaoh may issue against them ahead of time.", "reasons": "Al-Nahhas supplies an omitted 'act'; Abu al-Baqa supplies 'statement.' Al-Alusi regards this ellipsis as contrary to the apparent meaning, and al-Samin prefers Pharaoh himself as subject."}]}

{"id": "20:45/q10", "question": "How is يَفْرُطَ read?", "turns_on": "Differences in vowel pattern and verbal form yield haste, excessive harm, or an agent causing haste.", "positions": [{"id": "20:45/q10/p1", "position": "The majority read yafruṭ with fatḥa on yāʾ and ḍamma on rāʾ.", "reasons": "Ibn Atiyya and Qurtubi call this the majority reading and explain it as Pharaoh hastening to harm; the forerunner to water illustrates the sense."}, {"id": "20:45/q10/p2", "position": "Some read yufriṭ with ḍamma on yāʾ and kasra on rāʾ.", "reasons": "Ibn Atiyya assigns it to a group; Ibn al-Jawzi names Abd Allah ibn Amr, Ibn al-Sumayfi, Ibn Yaʿmar and Abu al-Aliya; Qurtubi names Ibn Abbas, Mujahid, Ikrima and Ibn Muhaysin; Abu Hayyan, al-Samin and al-Alusi give further group or al-Zaʿfarani transmissions. The sense is excessive harm, with some explanations allowing improper speech; Qurtubi cites rajaz."}, {"id": "20:45/q10/p3", "position": "Some read yufarraṭ or yufraṭ with ḍamma on yāʾ and fatḥa on rāʾ.", "reasons": "Ibn Atiyya and Qurtubi report Ibn Muhaysin; Ibn al-Jawzi also names Abu Rajaʾ. Abu Hayyan names Yahya, Abu Nawfal and Ibn Muhaysin; al-Samin and al-Alusi report the same readers. The passive or causative explanation is that an agent drives Pharaoh to haste; Abu Hayyan also allows excessive punishment."}, {"id": "20:45/q10/p4", "position": "Some read yafraṭ with fatḥa on both yāʾ and rāʾ.", "reasons": "Ibn al-Jawzi names Ikrima and Ibrahim al-Nakhaʿi; Qurtubi reports Ibn Muhaysin and al-Mahdawi's suggestion that the form is dialectal."}]}
{"id": "20:45/q11", "question": "What may Pharaoh's يَطْغَىٰ involve?", "turns_on": "Whether the feared transgression is violence toward the messengers, increased defiance or unbelief, oppression of Israelites, or offense against God.", "positions": [{"id": "20:45/q11/p1", "position": "He may exceed bounds in attacking, mistreating, or killing Moses and Aaron.", "reasons": "Wahidi says tyranny exceeds limits in mistreating them, and al-Kalbi and al-Mawardi specify killing. Al-Dahhak glosses aggression or transgression. Bursevi allows tyranny against the brothers with the preposition omitted for the verse ending, comparing 93:3. Islahi includes killing and plotting."}, {"id": "20:45/q11/p2", "position": "He may become more arrogant, defiant, and uncontrollable.", "reasons": "Al-Thaʿlabi reports arrogance and defiance; Ibn al-Jawzi attributes defiance to Muqatil. Al-Biqaʿi says Pharaoh may surpass his existing arrogance; Islahi says he may become more rebellious before the brothers can speak."}, {"id": "20:45/q11/p3", "position": "He may commit a graver offense against God or the sacred.", "reasons": "Razi says he may utter what is improper about God; Baydawi and Bursevi connect it with audacious, harsh speech. Al-Taʾwilat al-Najmiyya fears insults to God's commands. Tabatabai includes unprecedented daring against the sacred."}, {"id": "20:45/q11/p4", "position": "His disbelief may increase as he rejects or attempts to refute their proofs.", "reasons": "Tabrisi says he might kill before weighing the proof and reject in increased disbelief. Study Quran reports increased disbelief through attempted refutation."}, {"id": "20:45/q11/p5", "position": "He may intensify oppression of the Israelites.", "reasons": "Tabatabai includes worsening their punishment as part of the feared tyranny."}]}
{"id": "20:45/q12", "question": "Why is the second fear left open and placed last?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "20:45/q12/p1", "position": "The wording alludes discreetly to Pharaoh's potential offense against God, and saves the graver concern for last.", "reasons": "Zamakhshari describes the unqualified phrase as courteous restraint. Razi compares the hoopoe ending with the people's sun worship (27:24); Bursevi says the wording politely avoids saying 'against God' and ends with the greater offense."}]}
{"id": "20:45/q13", "question": "What does the repeated أن after أو convey?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "20:45/q13/p1", "position": "It marks both feared alternatives as live possibilities and gives them special weight.", "reasons": "Al-Alusi says أو keeps either alternative from being excluded and the explicit second أن, though unnecessary to basic sense, signals special concern. Al-Burhan records the hamza-before-waw form in Hud, Bani Israil, Ta Ha and al-Muʾmin, citing examples in Hud and al-Muʾmin."}]}
{"id": "20:45/q14", "question": "How does قالا introduce the response to the preceding command?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "20:45/q14/p1", "position": "It is an explanatory resumption stating what the brothers said after receiving the command.", "reasons": "Al-Alusi reads قالا as answering the implied question created by the preceding instruction."}]}
{"id": "20:45/q15", "question": "How does this fear fit the surrounding mission narrative?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "20:45/q15/p1", "position": "The difficult command to confront Pharaoh leads to the brothers' fear and God's reassurance.", "reasons": "Ibn Ashur says God showed Moses two signs, then assigned confrontation with the mightiest ruler; 20:45–46 recount fear and reassurance. Samarrai notes that Ta-Ha presents the joint mission throughout: both are sent, fear, reassured, deliver the message, and face Pharaoh together (20:29, 20:42, 20:63, 20:90, 20:92)."}]}
{"id": "20:45/q16", "question": "What is known of Moses and Aaron's journey and meeting before the mission?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "20:45/q16/p1", "position": "Moses traveled alone from the mountain to Egypt in severe want; Aaron then met him after revelation directed him to do so.", "reasons": "Bursevi's travel report says Moses lacked route knowledge, provisions, mount and companion, living on sparse fruit and game. Kashifi says Aaron met him on the road, heard the story and warned of Pharaoh's power. Ibn al-Jawzi reports Aaron was in Egypt when summoned."}]}
{"id": "20:45/q17", "question": "Why must the mission present proof completely?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "20:45/q17/p1", "position": "Complete presentation allows the proof to take effect and establishes accountability.", "reasons": "Tabatabai says omitting complete evidence for the wretched would defeat the testing account (17:82).
